lessons.title: Gross Rental Yield: The Headline Number and How to Calculate It

children.text: A broker in Bengaluru sends this on WhatsApp: "Ready 2BHK, Sarjapur Road, ₹1.08 crore. Rent ₹36,000. 4% yield, better than most flats in the city." The arithmetic is correct: ₹36,000 × 12 ÷ ₹1.08 crore is 4%. But once you use the rent the owner actually keeps and the price the buyer actually pays, the same flat yields about 3.2%. Nothing about the flat changed. Only the inputs did. By the end of this lesson you will know exactly which rent and which price belong in the formula, how to screen a listing in ten seconds, and the traps that make gross yields look better than they are.

body.text: Gross yield is only as honest as the two numbers you feed it. Use the rent you will actually receive and the full price you will actually pay, and a 4% pitch often turns into a 3.2% reality.

children.text: The Formula, Stated Precisely

body.latex: \text{Gross Rental Yield (\%)} = \frac{\text{Monthly Contracted Rent (excluding maintenance)} \times 12}{\text{All-in Acquisition Cost}} \times 100
body.caption: Gross means before your running costs: maintenance, property tax, vacancy, repairs and tax. Those come out in the next lesson.

children.text: Every word in that formula is doing work. "Contracted" means a rent someone has signed for, not a portal asking price. "Excluding maintenance" means only the money that is really rent. "All-in acquisition cost" means everything you pay to own the flat, not just the agreement value. Let us take the two halves one at a time.
Getting the Rent Right
Use signed rents, not asking rents.
Listings on 99acres, MagicBricks or NoBroker show what owners hope to get. Ask the society office, a local broker or a neighbour what similar flats in the same building actually rented for.

markDefs.definition: A rent quote where the owner pays the society maintenance out of the rent received, so part of the rent never reaches the owner.

children.text: Strip out maintenance.
A rent that is
inclusive of maintenance
is not comparable with one quoted "plus maintenance". On Sarjapur Road, ₹36,000 inclusive of ₹4,000 maintenance is really ₹32,000 of rent.

markDefs.definition: A refundable amount a tenant pays upfront as protection against unpaid rent or damage. It belongs to the tenant and must be returned.

children.text: The security deposit is not rent.
A
security deposit
is the tenant's money, held by you and returned at the end of the tenancy. It never goes into the yield calculation.
Use today's rent, not next year's.
An escalation clause of 5% a year raises future rent, but gross yield for a purchase decision starts with the rent you can sign for now.
A furnishing premium comes with a furnishing cost.
If you spend money on wardrobes, ACs and appliances to charge more rent, that spend belongs in the price side of the formula.

body.text: What about interest on the deposit? If the Sarjapur Road tenant pays a ₹1.92 lakh deposit (six months of rent) and you park it in an FD at about 6.5%, it earns roughly ₹12,500 a year, adding only about 0.1 percentage point to your return. Keep it out of gross yield. It is a small, temporary benefit on money you must give back.

body.title: What counts as rent?
body.question: You are calculating the gross rental yield on a flat before buying it. Which of these should NOT be included in the annual rent figure?
options: Rent for a covered car park that the tenant pays you separately
The extra rent charged because the flat is semi-furnished
The base monthly rent in the signed agreement
body.explanation: The security deposit is refundable and belongs to the tenant, so it is never rent. Car park rent, a furnishing premium and base rent are all real rental income, although any furnishing cost must be added to the price side of the formula.

children.text: Getting the Price Right

markDefs.definition: The total amount you pay to own a property: agreement value plus car park, stamp duty, registration, brokerage and legal costs.

children.text: The broker divided by the agreement value. But you cannot own the flat for ₹1.08 crore. Your real denominator is the
all-in acquisition cost

body.caption: Sarjapur Road 2BHK: from agreement value to all-in cost (illustrative)

cells: Stamp duty and registration (about 6.6% of ₹1.11 crore)

children.text: Now the honest calculation: ₹32,000 × 12 = ₹3,84,000. Divided by ₹1,19,61,000 and multiplied by 100, that is a gross yield of 3.21%. The broker's 4% was overstated by almost 0.8 percentage points, or about a fifth of the number.

body.title: The broker's yield vs the honest gross yield

columns.label: Broker's version: 4.0%
points: Rent: ₹36,000, including ₹4,000 the owner pays to the society
Ignores car park, stamp duty, registration, brokerage and legal costs
Useful for marketing, not for decisions

columns.label: Honest version: 3.2%
points: Rent: ₹32,000, the amount that is actually rent
Price: about ₹1.2 crore, everything paid to own the flat
Comparable across listings quoted in different ways
The right starting point for net yield in the next lesson

children.text: Once you own a property, the right price to use depends on the question you are asking.

body.caption: Which price belongs in the denominator?

cells: It is the money you will actually tie up.
Should I keep or sell a flat I already own?
Current market value, minus selling costs
That is the money you could free up and invest elsewhere today.
How has my original purchase worked out?
It measures rent against what you paid years ago. Good for reflection, misleading for decisions.

body.text: An under-construction flat has a gross yield of zero until possession. Any "expected yield on completion" is a forecast built on a rent you cannot sign for yet, often three or more years away. Treat it as a guess, and remember that pre-EMI interest during construction earns nothing at all.

children.text: The Ten-Second Screen: Rent per Lakh
When you are scrolling through fifty listings, you do not need a spreadsheet. Divide the monthly rent by the price in lakh to get the rent per ₹1 lakh of price, then use this shortcut.

body.latex: \text{Gross Yield (\%)} = \frac{\text{Monthly Rent per 1 Lakh of Price} \times 12}{1{,}000}
body.caption: Equivalently: every ₹100 of monthly rent per ₹1 lakh of price is a 1.2% gross yield.

children.text: American property investors talk about a "1% rule": monthly rent of at least 1% of the price, a 12% gross yield. Most Indian metro flats rent for roughly 0.25% to 0.33% of their price each month. That single comparison tells you how much of Indian residential property's return has to come from appreciation.

body.title: Screen a Thane listing
body.prompt: A 2BHK in Thane West is listed at ₹1.25 crore all-in, and similar flats in the building have signed rents of ₹38,000 a month plus maintenance. Using rent per lakh, what is the gross yield? Round to two decimal places.

body.title: The area trap: carpet area vs super built-up area

children.text: Builders and brokers often quote both prices and rents per square foot. That works only if both are on the same area basis. Since RERA, flats must be sold on carpet area, but many resale listings and rent quotes still use super built-up area, which includes a share of lobbies, lifts and clubhouse.

content.latex: \text{Gross Yield (\%)} = \frac{\text{Monthly Rent per sq ft} \times 12}{\text{Price per sq ft}} \times 100 \quad \text{(both on the same area basis)}
content.caption: Mixing carpet and super built-up figures can swing the answer by more than a percentage point.

children.text: The Sarjapur Road flat is 1,200 sq ft super built-up and 850 sq ft carpet. At ₹1.08 crore, that is ₹9,000 per sq ft super built-up, or about ₹12,700 per sq ft carpet. The ₹32,000 rent is about ₹26.7 per sq ft super built-up, or about ₹37.6 per sq ft carpet. Correct pairings give 3.6% either way on agreement value. But pair the carpet rent (₹37.6) with the super built-up price (₹9,000) and you get 5.0%. Pair the super built-up rent (₹26.7) with the carpet price (₹12,700) and you get 2.5%. Same flat, two wrong answers.

body.title: Is furnishing worth it?
body.scenario: Rahul owns the Thane West flat above, bought for ₹1.25 crore all-in and rentable unfurnished at ₹38,000 a month plus maintenance. A broker says: "Spend ₹3 lakh on wardrobes, ACs, a fridge and a washing machine, and you will get ₹42,000. That is ₹48,000 extra a year, a 16% return on the furnishing."
body.prompt: Calculate the gross yield before and after furnishing, check the broker's 16% claim, and decide whether the 16% is as good as it sounds.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Unfurnished: ₹38,000 × 12 = ₹4,56,000. ₹4,56,000 ÷ ₹1,25,00,000 × 100 = 3.65%.
2. Furnished: ₹42,000 × 12 = ₹5,04,000. The price side rises to ₹1,28,00,000. ₹5,04,000 ÷ ₹1,28,00,000 × 100 = 3.94%.
3. The broker's arithmetic is right: ₹48,000 ÷ ₹3,00,000 = 16%.
4. But the flat itself does not wear out in a few years, and furniture and appliances do. If they need replacing after five years, Rahul collects ₹48,000 × 5 = ₹2.4 lakh of extra rent, which does not even recover the ₹3 lakh spent. Over seven years, the extra rent is ₹3.36 lakh, only ₹36,000 more than the cost, before repairs.
5. So the 16% is not like a 16% FD. Most of it is simply Rahul getting the ₹3 lakh back slowly. Furnishing is worth it only if the premium is larger, the items last longer, or it meaningfully reduces vacancy. That vacancy question is exactly what the next lesson on net yield covers.

body.title: Calculate an honest gross yield
steps: Find signed rents for similar flats in the same building or lane, not portal asking rents.
Convert every rent quote to the same basis: rent excluding maintenance.
Leave the security deposit out entirely.
Build the all-in cost: agreement value, car park, stamp duty, registration, brokerage, legal costs and any furnishing.
Divide annual rent by all-in cost and multiply by 100.
If using per square foot figures, make sure rent and price are both on carpet area or both on super built-up area.

body.label: 99acres: rental listings
body.description: Good for a quick sense of asking rents in a micro-market. Always confirm with signed rents from the society or local brokers before calculating yield.

body.label: IGR Maharashtra
body.description: Maharashtra's registration department. Leave and licence agreements in the state must be registered, which makes it a useful public reference point for actual rents in Mumbai, Thane and Pune.

cards.definition: Annual contracted rent excluding maintenance, divided by all-in acquisition cost, times 100.
Agreement value plus car park, stamp duty, registration, brokerage, legal costs and any furnishing.
A rent quote where the owner pays society maintenance out of the rent, so the true rent is lower.
Refundable money held for the tenant. It is never part of rental yield.
Monthly rent divided by price in lakh. Every ₹100 of rent per lakh equals a 1.2% gross yield.
Carpet is usable floor area; super built-up adds a share of common areas. Rent and price per sq ft must use the same basis.

points: Gross yield = monthly rent excluding maintenance × 12 ÷ all-in acquisition cost × 100.
Use signed rents, strip out maintenance, and never count the security deposit.
Use the all-in cost, including car park, stamp duty, registration, brokerage and legal fees, not just the agreement value.
The same Sarjapur Road flat yields 4.0% in the broker's version and about 3.2% in the honest version.
For a buy decision use all-in cost; for a keep-or-sell decision use current market value.
Quick screen: every ₹100 of monthly rent per ₹1 lakh of price is a 1.2% gross yield.
A high return on furnishing can mostly be your own money coming back, because furniture wears out.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The people, properties, prices, rents and costs shown are illustrative. Stamp duty, registration charges and rental practices vary by state and change over time, so verify current figures and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making any decision.
